analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-style public health plan covering every American, funded by new payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: The Medicare for All Act drew 18 Democratic cosponsors in 2006 but was referred to three House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new 'Medicare for All' program: a public health plan offering every American benefits at least as good as what Members of Congress get, including prescription drugs, mental health parity, and children's preventive care. Enrollments phase in over about ten years — the youngest and oldest Americans first — and people can instead pick a contracted private plan, which is guaranteed payments and benefits matching the federal employee plan. It is funded by a new 1.7% tax on workers' wages and a 7% tax on employers' payroll, with the self-employed paying both.
analysis.who_benefits: People without reliable health coverage gain the most: the uninsured, people priced out of private plans, and low-income enrollees, who get reduced cost-sharing. Children under 20 and adults over 55 would be covered first, with everyone eligible by the program's eleventh year. People with mental illness gain from a strict parity requirement, and enrollees keep the choice of their own doctor under the public plan or can choose a regulated private plan whose benefits must match what federal employees receive.

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every citizen and lawfully present resident to a public plan covering the full range of Medicare Part A and B services, plus prescription drug coverage at least as broad as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield standard plan federal employees get, mental health parity, EPSDT children's services, and home and community-based care.

Guarantees benefits 'not less than' what Members of Congress receive under FEHBP, and phases in eligibility so people under 20 or over 55 are covered first, everyone by the eleventh year of the program.
Requires reduced cost-sharing for low-income enrollees at least as protective as Medicaid's rules, and lets people choose their own doctor and plan.
States the program's goals include ensuring all Americans have health care 'as good as their Member of Congress receives' and reducing the cost of health care.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would pay a new 1.7% tax on all wages and the self-employed a combined 8.7% tax on self-employment income; employers would pay a new 7% excise tax on every dollar of payroll. Both taxes apply to wages starting January 1 after enactment. Many employers already pay more than that for workers' health insurance and could drop those premiums, but small employers who do not offer coverage would take on a new cost. Enrollees in the public plan would still owe Medicare-style deductibles, copays, and premiums, not free care.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a new 1.7% tax on all wages, a 7% tax on employers' payroll, and an 8.7% tax on self-employment income, applying to wages on and after January 1 of the year after enactment — a permanent new tax burden before anyone is covered.

Universal coverage is slow: only people under 20 or over 55 are covered in the first five years, the next age bands in years six through ten, and everyone only in the eleventh year; no coverage begins for 18 months after enactment.
Coverage is limited to citizens and people lawfully present, leaving undocumented immigrants out.

The public plan keeps Medicare's cost-sharing — deductibles, coinsurance, copayments, and premiums — so it supplements rather than replaces out-of-pocket costs, and other public programs like Medicaid and VA must keep running alongside it as backstops.

Private plans in the program are paid the average per-capita cost of the whole program, risk-adjusted, which guarantees insurers a public revenue stream even if they enroll a sicker or less efficient mix of patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large: a guaranteed, comprehensive public plan that no American can be denied or priced out of, with explicit protections for the poor and for mental health care. The costs are real and the design is a compromise rather than a single-payer bill — new payroll taxes fall on everyone from day one while full coverage takes a decade to phase in, cost-sharing remains, and the bill deliberately keeps private insurers inside the program with guaranteed payments rather than displacing them. On balance it would transfer security to working people and their employers from the uninsured risk they carry today, but at a permanently higher tax burden and without eliminating private premiums and cost-sharing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees at introduction, then sent to a Ways and Means subcommittee two weeks later, and no committee ever took it up before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the Medicare for All Act on February 1, 2006, joined by 17 original cosponsors including Henry Waxman, Pete Stark, Sherrod Brown, and Barney Frank's Massachusetts colleague Michael Capuano-era Democrats such as Jan Schakowsky and Tammy Baldwin.
The Speaker referred it to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Government Reform, splitting its jurisdiction across three committees.
On February 17, 2006, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded; the bill received no further action through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained coverage, so the program's intended beneficiaries gained nothing from what actually happened. Health insurers and employers who would have faced the new payroll tax and the reorganized insurance market kept the status quo; the uninsured got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers; the uninsured gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican chairs of all three committees of referral took no action, and no vote was ever held to measure the split.

industries.note: Rather than displacing private insurance, the bill locks insurers in: the Secretary must contract with private plans, pay them the program's average per-capita cost (risk-adjusted), and require every FEHBP carrier to offer a plan on similar terms. Insurers keep a guaranteed public revenue stream even as the new public plan becomes the default and could draw enrollment away from employer coverage.

Employers would owe a new 7% tax on payroll, but many already pay more than that for employee health insurance and could drop those premiums; employers that do not currently offer coverage take on a genuinely new cost.

The bill creates a large new insured pool with a prescription drug benefit at least as broad as the federal employee standard plan, adding paying customers — though Medicare-style payment schedules could put downward pressure on prices.

More covered patients means fewer unpaid bills, but the public plan pays on Medicare fee-for-service rates, which are lower than typical private payments, and existing Medicare participation agreements would apply to the new program.
